tagline.text: Daet's June street festival celebrating the sweet Formosa pineapple

location.label: Location
location.text: Downtown Daet, Camarines Norte (the main streets and the town hall area)

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: Mid- to late June (about 10 days; dates change each year)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: 1–2 days (at least one day during the festival)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱2,500–7,000 (round-trip bus from Manila plus 1 night)

children.text: The Pinyasan Festival is a pineapple festival held by Daet, the capital of Camarines Norte, for about ten days in mid- to late June each year. Centered on the region's Formosa ("Queen") pineapple, it brings a street dance contest, a float parade, an agricultural fair and a pineapple cooking contest, and wraps up with the feast of Saint John the Baptist on June 24.
The Pinyasan Festival is held in Daet, the capital of Camarines Norte in the Bicol region. The name comes from
piña

, the Tagalog word for pineapple, and the star of the show is the small, sweet Formosa variety grown here, commonly called the Queen pineapple. It is said to have been first planned in 1993 by Tito Sarion, then a town councilor; it was originally called the Pineapple Festival and was renamed in 2003.
The festival usually runs for about ten days in
mid- to late June
and peaks around
June 24

, the feast day of Daet's patron saint, Saint John the Baptist. Sources give slightly different dates, such as June 15–24 or June 22–26, and the schedule changes from year to year, so be sure to check the latest announcement from the provincial government or Daet city hall for this year's dates. It overlaps with Daet's founding anniversary events, and the whole town is in a festive mood.

The attractions include a street dance contest in which teams in pineapple-inspired costumes dance to drums, a parade of floats shaped and decorated with pineapples, a fair of local farm products and specialties, a beauty pageant, sports events, and pineapple peeling and cooking contests. Pineapples and pineapple desserts are sometimes handed out free during the festival. Dances and costumes inspired by the culture of the local indigenous Kabihug people are also featured. The Queen pineapple is said to be special because it is small, intensely sweet and slightly tangy in a good balance. Some explanations credit Camarines Norte's soil and climate, and the practice of growing pineapples between coconut trees, for the sweetness. When people think of Philippine pineapples they usually think of the big plantations of Mindanao or Calauan in Laguna, but Daet's small Formosa has its own charm, and comparing the tastes during the festival is part of the fun of this trip.

Compared with the big national festivals, this is not an event built around tourists; it is closer to a provincial-town festival that the whole city enjoys together. There are no reserved seats or tickets to book, and the best way to enjoy it is to watch from the street and taste pineapple products at the market and street stalls. Since the trip from Manila takes around 7 hours by road, it works well as a 2-day/1-night to 3-day/2-night trip combined with the nearby Calaguas Islands or surfing at Bagasbas Beach in Bicol.

Teams in colorful costumes and headdresses shaped like pineapples march along the town's roads to drumming and compete in dance. The edge of the main road along the route is the best viewing spot; the afternoon sun is strong, so bring a hat and water.
Floats decorated with pineapples and farm produce pass by one after another. Each float has a different theme and is judged, so the decorations are polished and make for great photos.

During the festival an agricultural and industrial fair brings local products such as fresh pineapples, jam, pies and juice together in one place. There are plenty of good gifts, such as the pies from the Daet Food Producers Association, which combine pineapple jam and pili nuts in a pie crust. The fair is held during the day, and visiting in the quieter morning helps you avoid the crowds.
The pineapple cooking contest and the peeling race are fun to watch. There are sometimes chances to taste samples, so watch the mood on site and move closer.

The Formosa pineapple of Camarines Norte is known for being small, sweet and slightly tangy. Eating a small pineapple from a market stall yourself lets you feel the difference from fruit grown elsewhere.

blocks.title: Feast of Saint John the Baptist

children.text: The festival leads into religious events around the feast day of Daet's patron saint, Saint John the Baptist, on
June 24
. With Mass and processions at the church, you can see both the secular and the devotional sides of the celebration.
Bagasbas Beach, close to downtown Daet, is known as one of the Philippines' notable surfing spots. It is a good place to enjoy the sea and the sunset after watching the festival.

Good places to visit during breaks in the festival are all in town: the Parroquia de San Juan Bautista, founded in 1611; the Rizal Monument, presented as the world's first monument to José Rizal; and the Most Holy Trinity Cathedral.
Take the night bus to Daet from the Cubao terminal in Manila. Seats fill up fast during the festival, so reserve ahead.
Arrive at the Daet bus terminal, leave your bags at your accommodation and have breakfast at a restaurant in town. In the morning, walk the streets and soak up the festival preparations.
Find a spot along the main road before the parade starts. The times of the street dance contest and float parade differ each day of the festival, so check the local announcements.

In the gaps between parades, walk around the nearby church and the plaza in front of city hall. Daet has the Parroquia de San Juan Bautista, founded in 1611, and the first Rizal monument, both worth a short visit.
Taste pineapples and specialties at the market and the fair grounds, and have lunch.
Take a tricycle to Bagasbas Beach, stroll along the shore and watch the sunset.
Return to town for dinner, watch any evening events or performances, then rest at your accommodation.
Buy gifts such as pineapple jam and pies, then board the bus back to Manila.
The schedule changes with the festival program, so the above is only one example. Follow the on-site announcements for event times.
Arrive in Daet by night bus, rest in the morning, and spend the afternoon at the festival and market.
Watch the festival parade, then spend the afternoon at Bagasbas Beach.
If you want to add the Calaguas Islands, check the weather and boat schedules beforehand. The Calaguas Islands are covered in detail in a separate entry.
Boats may not run depending on sea conditions in the Calaguas Islands, so leave some slack in your schedule.

The most common way to reach Daet from Manila (Cubao) is a long-distance bus such as DLTB. Buses from Cubao are described as leaving in the morning and at night; schedules change, so confirm when you book.
Travel time varies greatly between sources, from about
6–7 hours
to nearly
12 hours
. Allow plenty of time for traffic.
Fares are listed at about
depending on the source. It varies by seat class and season.
In Daet, buses arrive at the Daet Integrated Terminal (Lag-on area).
Tickets sell out quickly during the festival, so book early, and have a printout or a screen ready because the terminal may ask for your reservation confirmation.
Daet has Bagasbas Airport, but you need to check the latest information on regular commercial service.
You can also fly to Naga City or Legazpi in Bicol and continue to Daet by bus or van. Flight routes and times change often, so check.
You can explore the town center on foot; for outlying places such as Bagasbas Beach, use a tricycle or jeepney.
Tricycle fares depend on distance and bargaining, so agree on the price before you get in.
The Pinyasan Festival is held every year in mid- to late
June
, so you need to time your visit for then. The exact dates change each year, and sources give different ones, such as June 15–24 or June 22–26, so always check the latest announcement.

Daet is hot and humid all year. Annual rainfall is high, and the wettest months are November and December; June is the start of the rainy season, so you may get showers. Bring a raincoat or umbrella and shoes that can get wet.

Downtown Daet has small hotels, guesthouses and motels, and near Bagasbas Beach there are places to stay aimed at surf travelers. Rooms fill up fast and prices rise during the festival, so reserve as early as you can and check recent reviews before choosing a particular place.

The star of the food is pineapple. It is sold fresh and also made into juice, desserts, jam and pies. As is typical of Bicol, dishes made with coconut milk and chili are easy to find in restaurants, so if you cannot handle spicy food, say so when you order.

In the evening, street stalls and late-night eateries tend to multiply around the town plaza. Pairing pineapple juice or a fruit dessert such as halo-halo helps shake off the fatigue of a hot day. During the festival, though, restaurants are crowded and prices may rise, so avoid lunch peak hours or line up early.

Daet is close to the sea, so the seafood is relatively fresh, and there are many chances to try Bicol-style dishes simmered in coconut milk. Dried fish and local snacks sold at the market also make good gifts.
Festival dates change every year, so confirm them through announcements from the provincial government or Daet city hall, or Department of Tourism materials, before booking transportation.
Bus travel times from Manila vary from 7 to 12 hours, so allow for arrival time and check your lodging's check-in time.
The sun is strong at street events. Bring a hat, sunscreen, water and comfortable shoes.
June brings frequent showers, so keep a folding umbrella or light raincoat in your bag.
Compare prices for specialties at the market and the fair booths, and for gifts choose items with sturdy packaging.
Roads get clogged on big event days, so get around mostly on foot and agree on a meeting point.
In a crowd, keep a close eye on your phone and wallet, and carry small bills.
Many stalls cut pineapples with a knife on the spot, so buy one and try it right there, and for gifts choose fruit with a firm rind.
Apart from the festival schedule, Daet is too far to visit from Manila in a single day, so plan at least one night and fix your return bus time in advance.
Dates and programs change every year and differ between sources, so be sure to check the latest announcement before booking.
Watch out for pickpockets on crowded days.
At the start of the rainy season, rain, road congestion and typhoon impacts can delay or cancel buses.
When you go to Bagasbas Beach to surf, follow the wave and rip current advisories and do not go into deep water alone.
Pineapple is acidic, and eating a lot of it can cause heartburn.
Some road sections are closed to vehicles during the festival, so public transport routes may change.
Many stalls and small lodgings need cash, so check ATM locations beforehand and carry small bills.
A white-sand island reached from Daet by land and then by boat. Boats cannot run when the sea is rough, so leave
1–2 days
of slack and check the weather.
One of the central cities of the Bicol region, about
2–3 hours
from Daet by road (it varies with traffic). It makes a good base for a Bicol trip.
A city with a view of Mayon Volcano, and a good place to combine with Daet in a Bicol itinerary.
A beach reached from downtown Daet by tricycle and known as a surfing spot. It is a good stop in the afternoon during the festival.
